identity.title: Sphinganine inhibits macrophage polarization and protects against sepsis-induced intestinal injury.

content.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sepsis-induced intestinal injury disrupts barrier function and exacerbates systemic inflammation, contributing to high mortality. AIM: To investigate the mechanism by which sphinganine protects against sepsis-induced intestinal injury, focusing on macrophage polarization and toll like receptor 2 (TLR2)/nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-kappaB) signaling. METHODS: A cecal ligation and puncture sepsis model was established in mice (n = 20/group). Treatments included sphinganine (15 mg/kg) and a TLR2 agonist [fibroblast-stimulating lipopeptide-1 (FSL-1), 10 mug/kg]. Serum markers [diamine oxidase (DAO), interleukin (IL)-1beta, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, IL-6] were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Intestinal injury and macrophage polarization [cluster of differentiation (CD) 86(+) M1, CD206(+) M2] were assessed via hematoxylin and eosin and immunofluorescence staining. Proteomic analysis, molecular docking, and Western blot were used to evaluate TLR2/NF-kappaB signaling. Data were analyzed by analysis of variance and t-test. RESULTS: Sphinganine significantly reduced serum levels of DAO (P < 0.05), IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, and IL-6 (P < 0.05), preserved intestinal crypt structure, and enhanced tight junction protein zonula occludens-1 expression. It promoted a shift from M1 (CD86(+)) to M2 (CD206(+)) macrophages. Proteomics identified TLR2 as the most differentially expressed protein, and molecular docking confirmed strong binding between sphinganine and TLR2 (-4.3 kcal/mol). Sphinganine downregulated TLR2 and phosphorylated-NF-kappaB p65 expression (P < 0.05), effects reversed by FSL-1. Total NF-kappaB p65 levels remained unchanged. CONCLUSION: Sphinganine protects against sepsis-induced intestinal injury by inhibiting TLR2/NF-kappaB signaling, modulating macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype, and preserving intestinal barrier integrity.
